soundcheck.heard: A mountain of rock near McCarthy, sped up twice, not once in the study, but twice each year. Sentinel-1 radar mapped seven rock glaciers near McCarthy from 2018 through 2022. They are rivers of rock and ice. Parts of sourdough peak moved more than 160 centimeters a year. A nearby glacier moved less than half as fast in the university summary. Photogrammetry checked more than 16,000 sourdough peak pixels. The maps correlated at .842, with mean error of 10.72 centimeters a year. Researchers fixed two components. Unsupervised separation yielded a long crawl and seasonal pulse they interpreted. That pulse peaked after snow melt and again with later rain. Four measured years lagged snow melt by 72 to 84 days. 2019 used an estimated 84 to 96 day temperature proxy instead. The measured surface signal is real. Is the explanation? The authors modeled a path from sunlight to melt water to a buried sliding layer. No borehole temperatures were recorded. The weather station sat six kilometers away. Two smaller glaciers broke the simple sunlight pattern. That does not erase the measurement. It turns the result into a sharper field test. Put sensors underground. Watch the next melt and rain. See whether the mountain keeps both appointments.
